name: Urge Surfing
plantPhilosophy: The lotus rests on water that never stops moving. It does not fight the current or sink into it — it stays on the surface and lets the water pass.

info.what: Noticing an urge and staying with it as a physical sensation until it passes, instead of acting on it or fighting it.
info.how:
1. Name it: "there's an urge."
2. Find where it sits in your body — chest, stomach, jaw, hands.
3. Describe it: hot or cold, tight or buzzing, still or moving.
4. Breathe normally and keep watching.
5. Notice it change. It will not stay at the same level.
info.when: Cravings, urges to gamble, urges to self-harm, sudden anger — any moment when a strong pull to act arrives and you have a few minutes before you would act.
info.why: Acting on an urge is what ends it fast, so your brain learns that acting is the only exit. Watching an urge without acting breaks that link. In a randomised trial, the programme built around this skill reduced substance use a year later. Note: it may not make the urge weaker — it changes what you do with it.

name: Delay and Distract
plantPhilosophy: Bamboo spends years growing roots underground before anything shows above the soil. Waiting is not doing nothing.

info.what: Putting a decision on hold for a short, set period, and filling that period with something absorbing.
info.how:
1. Say it: "not now — 15 minutes."
2. Set a timer.
3. Do one thing that takes your hands and attention: walk, wash dishes, call someone, prayer, a game.
4. When the timer ends, check in. Extend if you want to.
5. You are not promising forever. Only the next 15 minutes.
info.when: Early in an urge, while you can still move. Useful if sitting with an urge feels like too much at first.
info.why: Urges are tied to the moment and the place you are in. Putting distance between the trigger and the decision lowers the chance the decision gets made at full intensity. Used alone it becomes avoidance — pair it with another skill.

name: Knowing Your Risky Moments
plantPhilosophy: The banyan sends roots out across the ground long before it stands tall. It learns the shape of the land first.

info.what: Mapping in advance the people, places, times and feelings that reliably raise your risk — and deciding what you will do about each.
info.how:
1. List your last 3–5 close calls.
2. For each, write what was happening 30 minutes before.
3. Sort them: avoid for now / go, but with a plan / unavoidable, needs a skill.
4. Write one action for each.
info.when: At the start of a change attempt, after any slip, and before a known event — a wedding, payday, a family visit.
info.why: Specific situations, not general weakness, are what most often come immediately before a return to use. Removing a trigger is more reliable than resisting it, because it does not depend on how tired or stretched you are that day.

name: Saying No
plantPhilosophy: Pandan has a sharp edge along every leaf. It gives freely and it is still not easy to take from.

info.what: A short, practised, repeatable way to refuse an offer — the words, the voice, and an exit.
info.how:
1. Pick your line and keep it short: "No thanks, I'm not drinking."
2. No long explanation — explaining invites negotiation.
3. Say it with eye contact and a steady voice. No apology.
4. Offer something else or change the subject.
5. Have an exit ready. Use it if they push twice.
6. Rehearse out loud beforehand, ideally with someone playing the pressure.
info.when: Any situation where use is offered — especially with people who have a stake in you saying yes.
info.why: In one large alcohol trial, people who practised refusal had fewer drinking days, and the reason was that they came to believe they could do it. That is why rehearsing out loud matters more than reading. It does not work for everyone — one trial with adolescents found no benefit.

name: Slow Breathing
plantPhilosophy: The frangipani opens slowly and keeps its scent through the night. Nothing about it is hurried.

info.what: Slowing your breathing to about six breaths a minute, with the out-breath longer than the in-breath.
info.how:
1. Sit upright.
2. Breathe in through the nose for a count of 4.
3. Breathe out for a count of 6.
4. Normal size breath — slower rate, not bigger breaths.
5. Continue 2–5 minutes.
6. If you feel light-headed, go back to normal breathing. That means the breaths are too big.
info.when: Rising anxiety, anger, panic, restlessness, trouble sleeping. Also as a first step before trying a harder skill. Nobody can tell you are doing it.
info.why: Breathing at this rate measurably shifts your body toward its rest state — this is one of the most consistently confirmed findings in this whole set. It changes how your body feels now. It is not a cure for anxiety.

name: Cold on the Face
plantPhilosophy: Mint cools whatever it touches. It does not solve anything — it makes the next moment bearable enough to think in.

info.what: Briefly putting cold on your face to trigger a reflex that slows your heart. A reset that buys you access to your other skills.
info.how:
SAFETY FIRST — do not use this without medical advice if you have a heart condition, a low heart rate, high or low blood pressure, an eating disorder, or take beta-blockers.

1. Fill a bowl with cold water, or use a cold wet cloth or a wrapped ice pack.
2. Hold your breath.
3. Apply the cold around your eyes and upper cheeks, or lean your face into the bowl.
4. Hold 15–30 seconds.
5. Come up and breathe. Repeat once or twice if needed.
info.when: Only for very high distress — the point where you cannot think clearly enough to use anything else.
info.why: Cold on the face while holding your breath triggers a built-in reflex: your heart slows and your body shifts toward its rest state. The physiology is well established. Direct research on it as a coping skill is still limited.

name: Muscle Release
plantPhilosophy: The fern grows coiled tight, then opens. It cannot unfurl without having been curled first.

info.what: Tensing a muscle group, then releasing it, working through the body — and noticing the difference between tense and loose.
info.how:
1. Start at your hands. Clench for 5 seconds.
2. Release, and notice the change for 10 seconds.
3. Move up: forearms, shoulders, jaw, stomach, legs, feet.
4. Breathe out as you release.
5. Full body takes 10–15 minutes. Hands, shoulders and jaw alone takes 2.
info.when: Tension you carry in your body, trouble falling asleep, background stress. Best as regular practice rather than a crisis tool — it works better once it is familiar.
info.why: Across a large body of research it reduces stress, anxiety and poor sleep, likely by lowering muscle tension and physical over-arousal. Most of the strongest studies were in medical patients rather than in recovery settings.

name: Grounding
plantPhilosophy: Vetiver is grown on slopes to stop the soil washing away. Its whole value is in the roots, not what shows.

info.what: Using your senses to pull your attention out of your head and back into the room.
info.how:
Name, out loud or silently:
5 things you can see
4 things you can feel — chair, floor, fabric, air
3 things you can hear
2 things you can smell
1 thing you can taste

Go slowly. Repeat if you still feel far away.
info.when: Panic, feeling unreal or detached, a memory surfacing, the wired feeling after a shock. Also a safe way out of any exercise that becomes too much.
info.why: Attention is limited. Filling it with real things around you leaves less room for the spiral inside. This exact exercise has not been tested on its own — it is used because clinicians consistently find it helps, not because a trial proved it. If distress is severe or getting worse, contact the L.I.S.A. Helpline.

name: Checking the Thought
plantPhilosophy: Kaca piring is named for glass. A thought is worth looking through, not just believing.

info.what: Catching the thought driving a feeling, then testing it against evidence instead of accepting it or arguing with it.
info.how:
1. Write the situation in one line.
2. Write the thought exactly as it arrived — "I've ruined everything."
3. Rate how much you believe it, 0–10.
4. Write what supports it.
5. Write what does not fit it.
6. Write a version that accounts for both.
7. Rate your belief again.
info.when: Repeating self-attacking thoughts, all-or-nothing thinking, and thoughts that give permission to use — "one won't hurt," "I've earned this."
info.why: Changes in thinking and coping are one of the main routes through which therapy reduces use. Step 6 is a version that accounts for both — not a positive version. A reframe that denies real difficulty stops being believable, and stops helping.

name: Opposite Action
plantPhilosophy: The sunflower turns its face toward the light. It is a movement, made daily, not a feeling.

info.what: When an emotion pushes you toward something that will make things worse, doing the opposite — fully.
info.how:
1. Name the emotion.
2. Name what it is pushing you to do — hide, lash out, use, stay in bed.
3. Ask: does acting on this fit the facts, and will it help?
4. If no, find the opposite: approach instead of avoid, gentle instead of attack, get up instead of stay down.
5. Do it all the way — posture, voice, face included. Half-doing it does not work.
info.when: Shame that says isolate. Anxiety about something that is not actually dangerous. Low mood that says stay in bed. Anger that says send the message.
info.why: Every emotion comes with an action it wants from you. Following that action tends to feed the emotion; doing the opposite tends to shrink it. This is for emotions that do not fit the facts — if the fear is warranted, listen to it.

name: One Good Thing
plantPhilosophy: Gemitir is picked for the offering every morning, whether or not the day feels worth marking. The act comes first.

info.what: Deliberately putting one meaningful or rewarding activity into your day, planned in advance — whether or not you feel like it.
info.how:
1. List activities that used to matter, or still do. Small ones count.
2. Pick one.
3. Give it a specific slot: day, time, place.
4. Do it whether or not motivation arrives.
5. Rate your mood before and after.
6. Build up to a few per week.
info.when: Flat or low mood, empty days, and the stretch after stopping when life feels blank because use was the main source of reward.
info.why: Doing comes first, feeling comes second — waiting for motivation keeps the loop closed. This has strong evidence for low mood on its own. For people managing low mood and substance use together, the research is mixed, so treat it as worth trying rather than proven.

name: If–Then Plans
plantPhilosophy: The four o'clock flower opens at the same hour every day. It does not decide each afternoon — the cue does it.

info.what: Deciding in advance the exact situation and the exact response, in one sentence, before the situation arrives.
info.how:
1. Pick one risky situation you already know about.
2. Write: "IF [specific trigger], THEN I will [specific action]."
3. Make the trigger something you can actually notice — "if I walk past the shop on the way home," not "if I feel tempted."
4. Attach it to something already in your day rather than a clock time.
5. Say it, write it, put it where you will see it.
info.when: Anything you keep meaning to do but forget in the moment. This skill targets forgetting, not willpower.
info.why: Across dozens of studies, writing plans in this form has a solid effect on actually following through. The trigger becomes linked to the response in your memory, so it comes to mind on its own instead of needing to be remembered. This is the strongest evidence in the whole set.

name: Tracking
plantPhilosophy: The teak tree keeps a ring for every year, wet ones and dry ones alike. It does not choose which years to record.

info.what: Recording what actually happens — urges, mood, use, skills tried — instead of relying on memory.
info.how:
1. Pick two or three things to log.
2. Log close to when it happens, not at the end of the week.
3. Keep it short — a number and a word.
4. Log hard days with the same detail as good ones.
5. Look back weekly for patterns: times, places, feelings that repeat.
info.when: Ongoing, from the start. Most useful for spotting patterns you cannot see from inside a single day.
info.why: Writing things down builds awareness and shows you progress you would otherwise not notice. In substance use specifically, daily logging of use and mood has been linked to more abstinence and stronger coping. Log the difficult days too — a record with the hard parts removed cannot show you anything.

name: Reaching Out
plantPhilosophy: Mangroves grow with their roots tangled into each other. That is how they hold a shoreline that no single tree could hold.

info.what: Contacting a specific named person, before you need them, with a specific ask.
info.how:
1. Name 2–3 people in advance and write them down.
2. Decide what you would say — "I'm having a hard night, can you talk for ten minutes?"
3. Ask for something concrete: company, a call, a distraction, a ride away from somewhere.
4. Reach out early, not at the peak.
5. If nobody answers, the L.I.S.A. Helpline is open 24 hours, in both languages.
info.when: Isolation, shame, and the point where an urge is building and you are alone. Also as regular maintenance — not only in crisis.
info.why: Staying connected to other people is consistently linked to staying engaged with support and coming back after setbacks. Whether it directly changes use is still being studied — but it reliably keeps people in reach of help.

name: After a Slip
plantPhilosophy: A banana plant fruits once and falls. But it has already grown a shoot beside it, and that one is the same plant, continuing.

info.what: Treating a slip as an event with causes you can look at, rather than as proof about who you are.
info.how:
1. Stop the episode. Getting through the next hour matters more than understanding it.
2. Get somewhere safe and tell one person.
3. When you are steadier, write what happened in the hour before — where, who, what feeling.
4. Name the situation, not a verdict about your character.
5. Pick one thing to change, and make one if–then plan for that exact situation.
6. Go back to your routine the same day if you can.
info.when: After any slip — and ideally learned before one happens. This lesson is worth much less if it is first read afterwards.
info.why: When a slip gets explained as "I have no willpower" or "this is just who I am," shame and hopelessness follow, and a single slip is far more likely to become a full return to use. Looking at the situation instead is not making excuses — it points at something you can change. Character explanations do not.
